story_text.value:
Hey HN, I'm the solo developer behind Taskless. I built it because I got tired of praying AGENTS.md, .cursor/rules, etc. were getting followed. It's really annoying (and expensive) to fix stuff in later turns.

The CLI (MIT, https://github.com/taskless/cli) works with your local agent to read PR comments, fixup commits and agent files, find the corrections that keep coming up, and write them as ast-grep rules for code or Vale rules for prose. A model writes each rule once, and after that there's no LLM in the check. If your linter can already do the job, it uses your linter.

Things I really like about what I've built:

- Cross-file checks. The same static analysis tools that work on a single file can be used by scripts to check cross-file invariants. ast-grep captures what a rule cares about in each file, then a small TypeScript check gets all of those captures at once, so "every env var is declared in the TOML" becomes testable.

- Real fixtures. A cross-file / cross-language rule by definition needs more than one file to prove it works, so fixtures are whole directory structures. Every fixture goes through your agent and a deterministic sweep in the CLI before the rule is recorded.

- It generates cool reports. Because convincing your boss that you can use linter technology to reduce coding agent errors means less babysitting.

I ran it on some repositories I respect, and still found some improvements based on recurring PR comments and their respective agent and convention markdown files.

n8n: https://tskl.es/gh/n8n-io/n8n/20261026/1C3I3yVjFyfxNFEpl4qFA...

Effect: https://tskl.es/gh/Effect-TS/effect/20261104/1g4gRoMmoADlysg...

Pre-empting the privacy question, onboarding makes a shareable report like the ones above at a random impossible to guess URL, and you can delete it right away (it was just nicer than trying to read TUI output). Telemetry respects DO_NOT_TRACK=1 and TASKLESS_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1.

To try it, run npx @taskless/cli and ask your agent to set up Taskless.

Please poke holes in the CLI and the skill. I used a lot of determinism in onboarding to keep the agent from wandering and guessing, and I'd like to know where that helps and where it gets in your way.

title.value: Show HN: Taskless, turning AGENTS.md and PR comments into static analysis checks

story_text.value:
Hello HN,

I built `atl`, a Rust CLI for Jira, Confluence, Bitbucket, Jira Service Management, Trello and Atlassian Admin. The same commands work on Cloud and Data Center (on-prem).

It's built for both people and AI agents: an --agent mode that outputs JSON and never prompts, a built-in MCP server with 136 tools, and a read-only login so an agent can't change anything. Confluence pages can be edited as Markdown and kept in git.

It has SDK support as well for Python, TypeScript/JS, and WASM.

Any feedback and contributions are welcome!

title.value: Show HN: atl, a Rust CLI for Jira, Confluence and Bitbucket with ~15ms overhead

story_text.value:
Hi HN, we’re building Widefleet for teams building internal apps and workflows with coding agents.

Think Vercel or Cloudflare, with company login (SSO), app sharing, and controls for IT to manage who can access each app and which company systems it can connect to. Apps run as separate workers with per-app databases and object storage. You can also fully customize and manage connectors to internal systems, so your other users don’t have to handle API keys etc. themselves. Cron jobs and queues support background tasks and recurring workflows.

There’s now a hosted version, so give it a try and let us know what you think!

Try it: https://app.widefleet.com Code: https://github.com/widefleet/widefleet

Curious how you’re dealing with vibe-coded apps at work, whether you built them yourself or ended up maintaining someone else’s.

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

Here to show off a project that took 18 months, 7KLOC, and more importantly, 194 kilometres of walking! In a nutshell, I wanted to make the famous silhouette animation “Bad Apple” with Strava, which is an exercise tracking app that visualizes where you walk/run on a map. To use the earth as my canvas, I had to do a lot of coding in the prep work to plan where I would walk for each frame of the animation. As I explain in the video, my problem solving/coding steps were something like this:

- split video into frames, determine a good framerate

- detect contours with OpenCV for each frame. Since frames are very diverse, I had to start with some heuristics for choosing contours and ultimately make a GUI to manually curate all 438 of them (e.g. some frames had many small contours while others had a few important ones, and the video is constantly inverting colours). Output of this work was an intermediate json list of x,y coordinates representing the path along contours

- convert these cartesian coordinates into the Universal Transverse Mercator coordinate system, which represents the earth in a cartesian system (as opposed to GPS which doesn’t lend to adding relative distances in degrees very well)

- convert UTM to GPS using a package, then to the GPX file format which is universally accepted

- Import GPX files into an app that shows where I am and where I need to walk (I used Gaia GPS). Then I turned on Strava in the background and walked for ~18 months until this was done.

I also had to make a bunch of custom software to visualize these walks and make montages of them, like a script to pull polylines from the Strava API, a custom polyline renderer, a script to censor my strava activities a bit, and much more. I’m so proud of this work, it feels like it stands out in a sea of code-only bad apple projects that have become easier to automate with AI, and I hope it can go down as one of the greats in the bad apple colossus of work!

Video: https://youtu.be/HxdQawDIlnU GitHub: https://github.com/kevinlinxc/badapple-strava

Happy to answer any questions!

title.value: Show HN: Bad Apple but it's Strava [video]

story_text.value:
I miss the serendipity of finding interesting new books when there used to be more bookstores with bigger selections of books. Maybe we can use HN to fulfill that function. Maybe we can do a monthly "What are you reading?" ask-HN, and do it in the middle of the month since we already have (What are you working on? Who wants to be hired, etc) on the 1st of the month.

So please share a recommendation if you're reading something interesting, doesn't necessarily have to be new, could be any topic not just techy stuff. I think we can surface interesting books to read and the serendipty of finding new books that we would not have known about.

story_text.value:
Hey HN,

There is an interesting ongoing tension in the discourse around the quality of AI-generated code and whether "coding is solved".

As an experienced but very average programmer, the powers that AI have unlocked for me are nothing short of incredible. At work I am far more productive, and personally I have created/generated software that I would never have been able to create. For example, I've created my own very functional DAW (Digital Audio Workstation) that has tight integration with specific hardware I own.

I'm wondering if we are past the point of "AI generates bad and unmaintainable code". My gut tells me that for the most part we are, and my reasoning for this:

A) AI agents are able to find and fix many issues that I would never have caught B) They are FAR faster than me C) They generate WAY more tests (admittedly, sometimes it's out of hand) D) If something starts to really go sidewise in terms of code organization, you can often use AI to do the refactoring and cleanup and re-testing while you are out for a walk or having dinner with your family...

We are still fairly early into this experiment though. Do you fear that AI is generating unmaintainable code? Is the industry going to have major problems in the future with technical debt that more use of agents can't get us out of?

Do you have tips for how to coach agents into creating code that is correct and maintainable long term?

title.value: Ask HN: Tips for maintainability of large software projects using agents?
